column4: The section ties giving to the growth of crops; this ayah commands spending from good things earned and from what the earth produces, while forbidding selection of inferior produce for charity.
After the command to spend from good produce, this ayah sets Satan's threat of poverty against Allah's promise of bounty, a specific reversal of the fear that giving diminishes provision.
This ayah says public charity is good but secret charity given to the poor is better and expiates sins; it adds a private form of the face-seeking gift in the section.
This ayah describes people spending wealth by night and day, privately and publicly, and promises reward without fear; it repeats the section's picture of giving wealth for God.
Those who withhold what Allah gave them from His bounty are warned that the withheld wealth will become a collar; this is a concrete reversal of the section's wealth given for purification.
This ayah condemns misers who urge others to be miserly and hide Allah's bounty, a social version of the section's withholding contrasted with the giver.
Water brings forth vegetation, grain, clustered dates, and gardens of olives and pomegranates; this is a direct rain-to-harvest scene matching the section's cloud-grown plants and yielding palm.

This ayah describes people assigning shares of crops and livestock to Allah and their partners, then misallocating the shares; it provides a concrete contrast to the section's due crop and sanctuary offering.
This ayah says belief and taqwa would open blessings from heaven and earth, but denial brings seizure; it joins the section's fearful giver and denier to the reversal of provision.
Noah calls his people to seek forgiveness, then promises rain from heaven and increased strength; it directly joins repentance to renewed provision and growth.

This ayah says those favored with more provision do not return it to those under their authority so they become equal; its own contribution is withheld surplus, while 16:72 continues with spouses, offspring, good provision, and denial of favor.
A town once secure and supplied from every direction denies Allah's favors and is made to taste hunger and fear; it reverses the section's fruitful herd and crop into scarcity after denial.
The command to give relatives, the poor, and the traveler their due uses the source section's root ء ت ي in a direct distribution of wealth, then forbids waste.
This ayah says that if people owned the treasuries of their Lord's mercy they would still withhold for fear of spending; it sharpens the section's contrast between generosity and miserliness.
Each community is given a rite in which God's name is mentioned over livestock He provided; it joins the section's sanctuary animal to provision from God.
Asked who sends water from heaven and revives the earth after its death, people answer Allah; it makes the source of the section's field-growth explicit.
Water is driven to barren land and crops grow for people and livestock to eat; this is a precise meeting of the section's rain-grown field and herds.
Those who recite, pray, and spend from God's provision are described as hoping for a trade that will never perish; this turns the section's gift into lasting return.
The next ayah promises full payment and an increase from God's bounty; 35:29 contributes the non-perishing trade, while this row contributes its promised return.
When told to spend from what Allah provided, the deniers ask whether they should feed those whom Allah could feed; this is a direct refusal of the section's voluntary giving.
This ayah places night and day, rain from heaven, and the revival of earth together; it connects the surah's night-day frame to the section's rain-grown field.
People are called to spend in God's way and some withhold; the ayah says the miser withholds from himself and contrasts human need with Allah's richness, matching the section's giver and miser.
The section uses the root س ع ي for the collector's work and for varied effort; this ayah says a person has only what he strives for, locating responsibility in each person's own action.
The earth is laid out for creatures, beginning a passage that names fruit, date palms, grain, and fragrant plants; it gives the section's cultivated field a wider scene.
Fruit and date palms with their sheaths are named as earth's yield, directly matching the section's palm and crop growth.
Grain with husks and fragrant plants complete the yield; the ayah makes the earth's provision concrete in crops.
The ayah asks what people sow, introducing a direct crop image behind the section's growth language.
It asks whether people make the crop grow or God does; this makes explicit that the section's growth of field, palm, and giver comes from divine nurture.
God could make the crop dry debris after it grows; this gives the field's increase a specific limit and reversal.

This ayah directs distributed wealth to the Messenger, relatives, orphans, needy, and traveler so it will not circulate only among the rich; it extends the section's alms collection into social distribution.
This ayah warns believers not to let wealth and children divert them from remembering Allah; it identifies one way property defeats its owner, while 63:10 adds the urgency to spend before death.
The command to remind whoever benefits from reminder matches the surah's warning that precedes the giver's purification and the contrast with the denier.
This ayah says the one who fears will take the reminder, matching the section's giver among the God-fearing and the surah's promised ease.
The next ayah says the most wretched will avoid the reminder, completing 87:10's division between the one who fears and the one who turns away as in the section's two paths.
The section's surah ends by saying the giver will be satisfied; this ayah addresses the tranquil soul returning to its Lord, carrying the same stance into the closing scene.
The soul is described as satisfied and pleasing to God, a close counterpart to the section's promise that the giver will be content.
The satisfied soul is invited among God's servants; 89:28 contributes its approval, and this row contributes belonging to the company of the accepted.
The next invitation is to enter God's garden, completing 89:27-29's return and approval with the promised destination.
The ayah says the human being transgresses, setting up the section's description of one who becomes self-sufficient and withholds.
The specific cause is that a person sees himself as self-sufficient; this directly parallels the source surah's root غ ن ي in its description of the miser's imagined independence.
The ayah says the return is to the Lord, a boundary on imagined self-sufficiency that completes the section's contrast between worldly wealth and the giver seeking his Lord's face.
